headings.title: Medical Asepsis and the Role of Gloves
headings.content: Medical asepsis, often called clean technique, involves practices designed to reduce the number of microorganisms and prevent their spread in healthcare settings. While thorough hand hygiene remains the single most effective barrier against infection, gloves serve as an essential secondary line of defense. They protect both the healthcare worker from patient body fluids and the patient from transient microorganisms carried on the nurse's hands. However, gloves never replace handwashing; hands must be decontaminated both before putting on gloves and immediately after taking them off. Treating gloves as a substitute for hand hygiene is a frequent error that leads directly to cross-contamination across clinical environments.

headings.title: Indications for Wearing Gloves
headings.content: Gloves are indicated whenever exposure to blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, non-intact skin, or mucous membranes is anticipated during patient care. Routine tasks requiring clean examination gloves include starting an intravenous line, emptying a urinary catheter drainage bag, providing perineal care, or handling clinical specimens. Conversely, gloves are unnecessary for routine activities that do not involve bodily fluids, such as taking a patient's blood pressure, feeding a stable patient, or adjusting an oxygen cannula. Unnecessary glove use wastes resources and often leads to relaxed hand hygiene habits among clinical staff.

headings.title: Types of Gloves: Examination vs. Surgical
headings.content:
- **Examination Gloves**: Non-sterile or sterile gloves used for routine patient care, diagnostic procedures, and minor non-surgical tasks where exposure to body substances is possible.
- **Surgical Gloves**: Strictly sterile gloves featuring specific sizing, longer cuffs to cover gown sleeves, and higher tensile strength, designed for invasive surgical procedures and sterile body cavities.

headings.title: Material Selection: Latex, Nitrile, and Vinyl
headings.content:
| Material | Key Advantage | Primary Limitation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Latex** | Excellent fit, tactile sensitivity, and elasticity | High risk of severe allergic reactions |
| **Nitrile** | Strong puncture resistance and chemical durability | Higher cost compared to basic vinyl |
| **Vinyl** | Inexpensive and completely latex-free | Poor elasticity and prone to tearing easily |

headings.title: Procedure for Proper Glove Donning
headings.content:
1. **Hand Hygiene**: Perform hand hygiene thoroughly using soap and water or alcohol-based rub before touching any packaging.
2. **Inspect**: Check the glove box and individual gloves for visible defects, rips, or expiration dates.
3. **Select Size**: Choose the correct glove size; ill-fitting gloves tear easily or impair finger dexterity.
4. **Insert Hands**: Slide hands into the glove cuffs, pulling them up smoothly over the wrist to cover the junction of the gown sleeve entirely.

headings.title: Safe Removal and Doffing Techniques
headings.content: Removing gloves incorrectly is one of the most common ways healthcare workers contaminate their own skin. To doff safely, grasp the outside of one glove near the cuff with the opposite gloved hand and peel it down, turning it inside out as it comes off. Hold this removed glove in the palm of your still-gloved hand. Slide the fingers of your bare hand under the wrist of the remaining glove, peeling it downward so that the first glove ends up nested inside the second. Immediately discard both into the appropriate waste container and perform hand hygiene right away.

headings.title: Common Errors and Prevention of Cross-Contamination
headings.content: Gloves give a false sense of security if handled carelessly. A major error is touching environmental surfaces, charts, or door handles while still wearing soiled gloves, spreading pathogens across the ward. Never wash or reuse single-use disposable gloves; alcohol and water degrade the barrier integrity of thin medical films. Furthermore, fingernails must be kept short because long nails puncture glove material easily during patient care tasks.

headings.title: Gloves in Standard and Transmission-Based Precautions
headings.content: In standard precautions, gloves are used as part of personal protective equipment for every patient when contact with blood, body fluids, non-intact skin, and mucous membranes is possible. When transmission-based precautions are implemented—such as contact precautions for resistant organisms like MRSA—gloves must be put on before entering the patient room and removed before leaving. Transmission-based isolation highlights that gloves protect against specific epidemiological threats requiring strict containment within the immediate patient care zone.
